syllabus.clause: what each acknowledgement mode risks on failover (lost commits vs stalled writes)

at.step: Predict: what does synchronous replication cost instead?

items.item: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default; a primary crash can lose transactions not yet replicated
synchronous replication confirms that all changes made by a transaction have been transferred to one or more synchronous standby servers
requesting synchronous replication makes each commit wait until confirmation the WAL was written to disk on both primary and standby
waiting for synchronous confirmation doesn't use system resources, but the transaction's own locks are held until confirmed
if the primary fails, the standby should begin failover procedures
triggering failover of a log-shipping standby runs pg_ctl promote or calls pg_promote()
with regular asynchronous replication, the primary does not wait for a replica to confirm an event was received
semisynchronous replication waits for just one replica to acknowledge it has received and logged the events
with AFTER_SYNC, failover should be lossless since every committed transaction would already be replicated
with AFTER_COMMIT, failover may involve data loss since the primary may have committed transactions the replica never acknowledged
if a semisynchronous replica doesn't acknowledge in time, a timeout occurs and the primary switches to asynchronous replication

Asynchronous and synchronous replication aren't a spectrum from 'bad' to 'good' — they're opposite answers to the same question (when is a commit actually safe?), and neither answer is free: one spends durability, the other spends latency.
'Fire and forget' doesn't mean the replica never catches up — it means the primary never waits to find out whether it did, which is exactly the gap a crash can expose.

The wait a synchronous commit pays isn't CPU time, it's round-trip time — the documentation's own 'minimum wait time is the round-trip time between primary and standby' is why synchronous replication punishes distance specifically, not load.

A stalled write under synchronous replication isn't just slow — the transaction's own locks stay held for the entire wait, so a slow or unreachable replica doesn't just delay one client, it can back up everyone waiting behind that lock too.

Semi-synchronous replication's own timeout fallback means it quietly becomes asynchronous the moment a replica goes slow or silent — the guarantee it offers is conditional on the replica actually keeping up, not unconditional the way its name suggests.

Promotion is a one-way door in this basic picture: once a replica is promoted to primary, the old primary (if it comes back) is not automatically still a primary — it has to be reintroduced as a new replica, or conflicting writes can happen on both.

This topic's own local measurement of synchronous_commit's cost is a genuine stand-in for the same acknowledgement wait a real synchronous replica adds, but it is not a replacement for the multi-host failover and lost-commit claims themselves, which stay sourced directly from the documentation (see FACT-CHECK.md).

The choice between modes isn't fixed per database — PostgreSQL's own synchronous_standby_names can be set per user, database, or dynamically per transaction, which is exactly how a real system applies synchronous replication only to the writes that are worth the cost.

Lag, the next topic's own subject, is what makes asynchronous replication's risk concrete and measurable: the size of an asynchronous primary's own potential data loss is directly proportional to how far behind the replica currently is.

This refresher's three modes (asynchronous, synchronous, semi-synchronous) describe acknowledgement timing only — they say nothing yet about what a replica actually ships (WAL bytes vs. decoded row changes), which is exactly what the next topic opens.
